name: Sparks

stops.name: Victorian Square
stops.teaser: A railroad town’s old-fashioned main plaza.
stops.map: Victorian Square, Victorian Ave, Sparks, NV
stops.clue: Find the plaza on Victorian Avenue with the train-themed shelter and a real steam locomotive on display. Sparks was a railroad town from day one, and the railroad is still the star here.
stops.safety: Stay on sidewalks and trails, away from the active rail yard and tracks, which are private and dangerous. Trains still run here. Cross streets only at corners.

then.line: This photo shows Southern Pacific No. 8 in Carson City in 1975. It is the same engine that Union Pacific says is now on loan here, shown in a different town, so this is a looser match, not the same spot.

now.head: Today
now.label: Victorian Square
now.line: The square keeps the railroad theme, with a train-style shelter on Victorian Avenue. Photo taken in 2011, so details may have changed.

story: Sparks began in 1904 when the Southern Pacific Railroad moved its terminal here from Wadsworth. The new town was named for Nevada governor John Sparks.
Victorian Square is the town’s historic heart. Union Pacific says it shows Southern Pacific Engine No. 8, on loan from the Nevada State Railroad Museum.
Sparks Heritage Museum sits nearby on Victorian Avenue, with local history from the railroad years.
stops.fact: The town was first called East Reno, then Harriman, before it was renamed for the governor in April 1904.
stops.disputed: The photo of Engine No. 8 here was taken in Carson City, not Sparks. The engine only came to Victorian Square later, so the “Then” is the same engine in another place, not the same view. The 2011 “Now” photo shows the shelter, not the engine itself.

claims.t: Sparks was named for a Nevada governor.
claims.why: Sources agree it was named for Governor John Sparks in 1904.

claims.t: Sparks has always been called Sparks.
claims.why: It was first called East Reno and then Harriman before the 1904 renaming.

stops.clue: Find the blue Nevada historical marker about the Southern Pacific rail yards. Look across to the yard. Big repair shops once stood here, and some of the work still goes on nearby.
stops.safety: Stay on sidewalks and trails, away from the active rail yard and tracks, which are private and dangerous. Trains still run here. Cross streets only at corners.

now.head: Today
now.label: The marker at the rail yard
now.line: The shops are mostly gone. A historical marker now tells the story. Photo taken in 2011.

story: In summer 1904 the Southern Pacific moved its terminal from Wadsworth to the new town of Sparks. Workers built a depot, a freight yard, and big shops.
The railroad was the town’s main employer for most of the next century. Passenger trains stopped here until 2009.
Part of the old machine shop was reported demolished in 2024.
stops.fact: The depot opened on June 19, 1904, and the building is now a yard office for Union Pacific.
stops.disputed: The state marker says the machine and erecting shops still stand, but Wikipedia says the machine shop was demolished in 2024. Check what you can see on site.

claims.t: The Southern Pacific moved its terminal to Sparks in 1904.
claims.why: Both the state marker and Union Pacific give 1904.

claims.t: Passenger trains still stop in Sparks today.
claims.why: Passenger service ended in 2009 per Wikipedia.

stops.clue: Head to the Tahoe-Pyramid Trail along the Truckee River, on the south side of town. Find a spot where you can see the water and the hills beyond it.
stops.safety: Stay on sidewalks and trails, away from the active rail yard and tracks, which are private and dangerous. Trains still run here. Cross streets only at corners.

q.prompt: Which famous lake does the Truckee River flow out of, upstream of Sparks?
q.hint: It is the big blue lake on the border of Nevada and California.
q.verify: Look for a trail sign or marker naming the river. Confirm what is posted on site.

then.label: River Scene, Sparks
then.line: The 1906 postcard is titled only “River Scene, Sparks, Nev.” The Truckee is the river here, so it is the likely match.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The Truckee along the trail
now.line: The Tahoe-Pyramid Trail follows the river between Sparks and Reno. Photo taken in 2020.

story: The Truckee River begins at Lake Tahoe and runs about 120 miles down to Pyramid Lake. It passes right along the edge of Sparks.
The river gave the railroad a path across the desert, and the town grew up beside it.
Today a paved trail follows the water between Sparks and Reno.
stops.fact: The Truckee does not reach the ocean. It ends in Pyramid Lake, which has no outlet.
stops.disputed: The postcard only says “River Scene.” It was probably the Truckee, but the exact spot is not known, so this “Now” photo is a match for the river, not the spot.

claims.t: The Truckee River flows out of Lake Tahoe.
claims.why: Lake Tahoe is its source, and it ends at Pyramid Lake.

claims.t: The Truckee River flows to the Pacific Ocean.
claims.why: It ends in Pyramid Lake, in a basin with no outlet to the sea.

stops.safety: Stay on sidewalks and trails, away from the active rail yard and tracks, which are private and dangerous. Trains still run here. Cross streets only at corners.

now.head: Today
now.label: Sparks Marina at sunset
now.line: The Marina is now a lake of about 77 acres with beaches, a pier, and a loop trail. Photo taken at sunset in 2012, with enhanced colors.

story: For decades the Helms gravel pit supplied rock for roads. In 1987, millions of gallons of oil leaked into the pit from a nearby tank farm.
The city bought the site in 1995. After a cleanup, the New Year’s Day flood of 1997 filled the pit with water in about two days, and it became a lake.
Today it is Sparks Marina Park, with the 77-acre Helms Lake and a loop trail.
stops.fact: The lake was filled by the 1997 flood in about two days, with roughly a billion gallons of water.
stops.disputed: The “Then” photo is a stand-in, not the pit. Sources also differ on small details of the cleanup, so check the details on site.

claims.t: The Sparks Marina lake started as a gravel pit.
claims.why: The Library of Congress and KUNR both describe the Helms gravel pit.

claims.t: The Marina was dug as a lake on purpose.
claims.why: It was a gravel pit, and the 1997 flood filled it with water.
